text: Chapter 11, the news feed system. In a few minutes, let's see how push and pull work.

A news feed does two jobs. Publishing: a post is written to the database, then spread to friends' feeds. Building: when a user opens the app, we gather friends' posts and return them in reverse chronological order. The scale is up to five thousand friends per user, and ten million daily active users.

First, publishing. The request goes through a load balancer to a web server, which authenticates the user and rate-limits. The post service then saves the post to the database and cache. Next, the fanout service pushes it to friends' news feed caches, and the notification service alerts those friends.

How does fanout work? It fetches the friend list from a graph database, then filters out anyone the user has muted or blocked. The friend list and the post ID go into a message queue. Workers consume the queue and add one entry to each friend's news feed cache. Only the post ID is stored, never a copy of the post. This is fanout on write: we push to readers at posting time.

Fanout on write makes reads fast, and updates arrive immediately. The cost shows up when a user has many friends. A regular user with a few hundred friends writes a few hundred small lists. But a celebrity with a million readers must update a million lists for a single post. That's write amplification.

Now fanout on read. When someone posts, we only store the post itself and push nothing. When a reader opens the feed, the system fetches the latest posts from each of their friends, then merges and sorts them. Inactive users cost nothing in advance, so writes are cheap. The price is many reads on every open, so reads are slower.

Let's compare the two. When a celebrity posts, push writes a million times, while pull writes once. When a reader opens the feed, push reads only their own cache, while pull must read from every friend they follow. Either way, the cost lands on the write side or on the read side.

A hybrid approach takes the best of both. Regular users' posts are pushed to their followers as usual. Users with huge followings don't fan out; their posts are stored once. When a reader opens the feed, we take their cache, pull the latest posts from the celebrities they follow, and merge. Both write amplification and read latency stay under control.

Finally, the read path. The request passes the load balancer and web server, then reaches the news feed service. It takes post IDs from the news feed cache, then fetches full posts from the content cache or the database. The cache holds only IDs, so results are filtered by current permissions at read time. Deleted posts and blocked authors must not appear.
Remember three words: push, pull, hybrid. Regular users push, big accounts pull, and the cache stores only post IDs.
